subject: anaesthesia
title: Neuraxial Complications: Post-Dural Puncture Headache, High Spinal, and Hypotension

steps.title: PDPH Pathophysiology and Presentation
steps.tx: **Post-dural puncture headache pathophysiology** results from continuous cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage through an unhealed dural puncture hole exceeding CSF production rates (normal production 0.35 mL/min or 500 mL/day). Loss of CSF cushioning drops intracranial pressure, causing gravitational downward sagging of the brain when upright. This sags pain-sensitive intracranial meninges, nerves (cranial nerves V, IX, X), and stretches the abducens nerve (CN VI).

steps.title: Postural Hallmark and Cranial Nerve Signs
steps.tx: **Clinical hallmark of PDPH** is its strictly postural character: severe fronto-occipital throbbing headache that erupts within 15 to 45 seconds of sitting or standing upright, completely resolving or improving dramatically upon assuming the supine horizontal position. Associated features include neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, tinnitus, and lateral rectus palsy with diplopia resulting from traction on the elongated intracranial course of the sixth cranial nerve.

steps.title: Risk Factors for PDPH
steps.tx: **Risk factors for post-dural puncture headache** are dominated by mechanical needle design and patient age: young adult females (particularly obstetric parturients aged 20 to 40 years) have high dural compliance and high CSF pressure, rendering them vulnerable. Cutting Quincke needles and large needle calibers (16-gauge or 18-gauge accidental epidural punctures cause 50 to 70% PDPH) multiply risk compared to 25-gauge or 27-gauge pencil-point Whitacre needles.

steps.title: Conservative Medical Management
steps.tx: **Conservative medical therapy for PDPH** encompasses bed rest in the comfortable position, aggressive oral and intravenous hydration, oral analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs, codeine), and intravenous or oral caffeine (300 to 500 mg orally or 500 mg IV caffeine sodium benzoate). Caffeine acts as a central adenosine receptor antagonist, producing compensatory cerebral vasoconstriction that counteracts intracranial compensatory venodilation.

steps.title: Epidural Blood Patch (EBP) Protocol
steps.tx: **Epidural blood patch definitive protocol** represents the gold standard curative intervention for moderate to severe refractory PDPH, boasting a 70 to 90 percent success rate on the first attempt. Under strict aseptic technique, an epidural needle enters the epidural space at or one space below the prior dural puncture site; concurrently, 15 to 20 milliliters of autologous blood is drawn sterilely from an antecubital vein and slowly injected into the epidural space.

steps.tx: The patient's own blood becomes the dressing in this cross section. Injected into the epidural space, it spreads over the torn dura and clots into the **blood patch**, sealing the leak while epidural pressure itself squeezes the defect shut from outside. Relief of the postural headache often arrives before the needle leaves the room. Fifteen to twenty millilitres is the usual volume, drawn sterile from the arm at the same sitting, making this a cure assembled entirely from the patient.
steps.say: An epidural blood patch seals the dural hole with the patient's own clotted blood, curing postural headache.

steps.title: High Spinal versus Total Spinal
steps.tx: **High spinal and total spinal emergency** occurs when local anaesthetic spreads cephalad above anticipated dermatomes: a high spinal (blocking thoracic T1 to T4 cardioaccelerator fibers) causes severe bradycardia, hypotension, dyspnoea, and upper limb numbness. A total spinal occurs when local anaesthetic enters the subdural space or ascends into the cervical spine and brainstem, paralyzing the diaphragm (phrenic C3-C5), provoking unconsciousness, apnea, and dilated fixed pupils.

left.title: High Spinal Blockade (T1 to T4)
points: Severe bradycardia and profound systemic hypotension

right.title: Total Spinal Blockade (C1 to Brainstem)
points: Ascends to cervical roots and medullary cardiorespiratory centers

steps.title: Emergency Total Spinal Resuscitation
steps.tx: **Emergency management of total spinal** requires swift, aggressive supportive resuscitation following airway, breathing, and circulation priorities: immediately tilt table head-up slightly if within 5 minutes (to arrest hyperbaric ascent), support airway with 100 percent oxygen, perform rapid tracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation, infuse rapid crystalloid boluses, and administer intravenous adrenaline or ephedrine and atropine for profound bradycardia.

steps.title: Post-Spinal Hypotension Management
steps.tx: **Spinal-induced hypotension mechanisms** result from preganglionic sympathetic vasoconstrictor nerve blockade (sympathetic denervation extending two to four dermatomes higher than sensory block), causing massive venodilation that pools blood in capacitance beds, dropping venous return, preload, and cardiac output. Treat with intravenous fluid coloading (crystalloid 15 mL/kg given during block placement), phenylephrine (alpha-1 agonist), or ephedrine.
